extracted.intended_audience: geometers, editors/translators of Euclid, and advanced students studying Euclidean foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Critical editorial and pedagogical notes on Books V–VI of Euclid's Elements, giving standards for legitimate demonstrations, correct definitions, treatment of ratios/compound ratios, and editorial practice. Aimed at improving proofs, enunciations, and definitions in editions/translations of Euclid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume unproved existence in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations must not rely on hypotheses about existence (e.g., 'that to any three magnitudes... there may be a fourth proportional') unless that existence has been proved previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a construction or existence claim (like the fourth proportional) is required by a proof, either prove it earlier or provide a legitimate construction within the proof; avoid assuming such existence 'without any proof' as this 'renders the demonstration of no force.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must follow only from prior demonstrations and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid 'never assumes anything in the demonstration of a proposition, which he had not before demonstrated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure demonstrations so every used fact is already established (definition, proposition, or lemma). Do not import unanalyzed intuitions; explicitly derive conclusions from the stated definitions and previously proved propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the distinction between magnitudes and ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'greater, the same, or equal, lesser' have different meanings when applied to magnitudes and to ratios; one must not transfer evident facts about magnitudes directly to ratios without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about ratios, use Euclid's definitions (especially the 5th and 7th of Book V) and show how magnitude comparisons translate into ratio comparisons via equimultiples; avoid informal appeals to 'what is manifest of magnitudes' for ratio arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle all logical cases explicitly in demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should include every possible case (e.g., the omitted 'third case' in a demonstration is criticised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposition naturally splits into cases (A greater than B, equal, or less), present and justify each case or give a construction that simultaneously covers them; omission of a genuine case makes a demonstration incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or superfluous constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce elements that 'serve to no purpose but to lengthen the demonstration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim constructions and steps that do not contribute to the logical flow; if a change made in different cases is redundant across cases, avoid repeating or adding it needlessly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enunciate propositions with appropriate generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements should be expressed to cover the correct general case (e.g., extending propositions 'to any number of magnitudes' rather than leaving them restricted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the mathematical content supports a general statement, phrase the enunciation to reflect that generality; conversely, avoid enunciations that ambiguously limit the scope and thereby force prolix demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authentic, clear, and pedagogically suitable definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should reflect Euclid's intent when possible and be clear for learners (the 2nd definition of Book VI 'does not seem to be Euclid's' and the 5th def. of Book VI 'has been kept... to the great detriment of learners').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions that are geometrical, historically authentic, and pedagogically lucid; replace obscure or evidently later insertions with clearer formulations (the text suggests improved wording for reciprocally proportional magnitudes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define compound ratio geometrically, not arithmetically
rubrics_metrics.description: Theon's definition of compound ratio (via multiplication of 'quantities' or 'exponents') is 'ungeometrical and useless'; compound ratio should be the compounding of intermediate ratios as in duplicate/triplicate definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a geometric definition: the ratio compounded of intermediate ratios (as in duplicate/triplicate) rather than defining it by multiplying numeric exponents or antecedents/consequents, which fails for nonnumeric ratios (e.g., diameter:side of square).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place the same substantive claim both as a definition and as a proved proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'absurd that the same proposition should stand as a definition in one place of the Elements, and be demonstrated in another place of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundancy where a truth is declared as a definition in one location and proved elsewhere; either make it a proved proposition or a definition, consistent with logical structure and teaching needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make demonstrations explicit and sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is criticised as 'not sufficiently demonstrated' when key implications are omitted (e.g., the 10th prop lacked proof that certain multiples relationships always hold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill in omitted intermediate steps that the original text implicitly relied upon; ensure every inferential leap, especially when moving from ratios to conclusions about magnitudes (or vice versa), is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve authentic method; avoid unskilful editorial alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors (e.g., Theon) have sometimes 'vitiated' propositions by changing demonstrations or introducing definitions not Euclid's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In editing/translating, prefer restorations that reflect Euclid/Eudoxus's method; resist introducing modernizations or shortcuts that change the original logical dependencies or obscure the geometric method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base ratio comparisons on equimultiples per Euclid's definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons of ratios should be carried out 'by the 5th def. of book 5' and the use of equimultiples/7th definition is central in proofs (frequent citations throughout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving statements about 'A has a greater ratio to C than B to C', use the standard equimultiples technique: produce equimultiples that show the requisite ordering, and rely on the formal definitions rather than informal numeric intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: When translating, restore sense rather than literal wording when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal translations from Greek may misstate sense (example: recommended reading of a phrase in Prop. XIII to reflect 'so that' rather than a literal 'is greater').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer translations that convey the logical sense of the original, even if this departs from word-for-word rendering; annotate literal renderings when they mislead and justify the chosen reading by reference to earlier editions or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add useful corollaries and extend propositions when they aid later use
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollaries are sometimes 'added' because they are 'as frequently used as the proposition itself' and extensions to broader cases make later application smoother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include corollaries or extended enunciations when they are frequently employed in subsequent propositions or demonstrations; such additions should be logically derived and clearly flagged as corollaries.
